strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned contribution: the paper convincingly identifies a real gap (poor textual quality in existing DyTAG datasets, lack of standardized generative task formulations) and provides the first dedicated benchmark for generative DyTAG learning.

Careful dataset construction: eight datasets spanning diverse domains and graph types (bipartite/non-bipartite), with detailed documentation, licenses, dataset analysis (degree/label distributions), and a systematic comparison with prior datasets (Table 11).

The empirical validation that text quality impacts structural generation quality (Figure 2/6-7: text features reduce Degree/Spectra MMD on GDGB but hurt performance on DTGB in half the cases) is a genuinely interesting and useful insight that motivates the benchmark.
Two clearly defined tasks (TDGG/IDGG) with formal algorithms and pseudocode, and a reasonable multifaceted evaluation protocol covering structural, temporal, and textual dimensions.
Extensive experiments: four LLM backbones, DGNN baselines, generation-model baselines, ablations on memory/reflection mechanisms, scalability analysis, and comprehensive results in the appendix.
Reproducibility effort: public datasets, code, leaderboards, full prompt templates, and implementation details provided.
weaknesses: Potential technical inconsistency in the proposed graph embedding metric: the metric is formally defined with 'Lower ρ values indicate higher global fidelity' (Appendix B.2), yet in Tables 4, 9, 25, 45, and 46 the bolded 'best' values are consistently the highest scores. Either the definition or the table interpretation is wrong, which undermines the paper's headline holistic metric and several conclusions drawn from it.

Circular/self-biased textual evaluation: LLM-as-Evaluator (with a GPT backbone, Appendix C.4) is used to score texts generated by four LLMs, and GPT-generated text wins on textual quality in nearly every configuration (Tables 3, 8, 16-24, 36-44). This self-evaluator bias is not addressed or mitigated (e.g., no human evaluation, no judge-LLM other than GPT, no validation of the 1-5 criteria against ground-truth text), and the criteria (Personality Depth, Immersive Quality) are borrowed from role-playing research and are of questionable relevance to graph generation.

The claimed superiority of GAG-General over DGNNs on discriminative tasks (Tables 5, 6) is not an apples-to-apples comparison: DGNNs are trained on only 1,000 edges while GAG-General's 'performance' is measured on its own generated graph relative to ground truth; the setup structurally favors the proposed method, and the Hit@10 results (Table 5) actually show DyGFormer dominating on most datasets, which contradicts the framing.

The IDGG comparison against VRDAG and DG-Gen (Table 10/46) is arguably unfair: baselines are trained on a 1,000-edge seed and lack generation-size control (VRDAG), so their very poor MMD/embedding scores may reflect setup mismatch rather than model limitations; no effort is made to tune or adapt baselines.

Graph embedding metric values are inconsistent across related settings (e.g., Cora: 0.828 in Table 46 vs. 0.572 in Table 45) with insufficient explanation, and textual quality scores cluster tightly (~4-5 on a 1-5 scale) with weak discriminative power across configurations.

Dataset quality issues: WikiLife temporal span is stated as '202 to 2024' (typo); IMDB extends to 2031 (future releases); WeiboTech covers only one week; the text of Section 5.3 references Table 2 while describing IDGG (Table 7). These errors raise concerns about curation rigor.

GAG-General is a relatively incremental framework contribution—mainly generalizing the existing GAG [25] beyond bipartite graphs—and the benchmark's main evaluated method comes from the authors themselves, which weakens neutrality of the benchmark's headline results.
Generated scale (2,000-10,000 edges) is tiny relative to the multi-million-edge datasets; how evaluation metrics behave at scale is largely untested despite the scalability claims.
Reproducibility links are placeholders ('available at here') and the LLM-based generation is expensive (16-36 hours for 50k-100k edges), limiting practical adoption and independent verification.

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: existing DyTAG benchmarks (e.g., DTGB) focus on discriminative tasks and contain low-quality node/edge texts, making them unsuitable for generation tasks. The motivation is well-articulated and supported by Figure 1/2 analyses.

The released resource is substantial: eight DyTAG datasets spanning multiple domains, both bipartite and non-bipartite, with detailed statistics, dataset analysis (degree/label distributions), license documentation, and stated availability of code and leaderboards.
The two proposed tasks (TDGG/IDGG) are clearly formalized, with pseudocode, prompt templates, and reproducibility-oriented implementation details in the appendix.

A broad experimental matrix is covered: four LLM backbones, ablations over node memory and reflection mechanisms, comparisons against five DGNN baselines and two dynamic graph generation models, plus scalability analysis.
weaknesses: Limited framework novelty: GAG-General is essentially a generalization of the existing GAG [25] (bipartite-specific LLM multi-agent generation) to non-bipartite graphs via prompt engineering. The three 'enhancements' (generalization, multi-domain compatibility, standardization) are incremental engineering rather than a methodological contribution, and the core generation pipeline, memory module, and reflection mechanism are inherited from prior work.

Circular and potentially invalid evaluation of textual quality: the generated texts are produced by LLMs and then scored 1-5 by the same family of LLMs (LLM-as-Evaluator with GPT backbone), with no human evaluation to validate the five criteria. The reported scores are tightly clustered (roughly 3.5-5.0), with tiny gaps between configurations claimed as 'significant improvements,' raising serious doubts about the discriminative power and validity of the headline textual-quality claims.

The edge-classification 'superiority' over DGNNs appears circular by construction: GAG-General generates the edge labels and edge texts together, so evaluating edge classification on its own generated graph rewards label-text correlation rather than genuine modeling capability. This comparison is not a fair test of the framework and the claimed insight ('GAG-General outperforms DGNNs') is not supported by sound methodology.

Inconsistencies in metric reporting undermine soundness: the graph embedding metric is defined such that lower ρ indicates higher fidelity, yet Tables 4, 9, 25, and 45 bold/highlight the highest values as best, and the paper's narrative treats improvements in either direction as favorable (e.g., Sephora DeepSeek 0.758 bolded over 0.679; GPT WeiboTech 0.698). Either the metric definition or the interpretation is wrong. There is also a typo referring to Table 2 where Table 7 is meant, and the WikiLife embedding value (0.804 in Table 45) is inconsistent with Table 9.

Comparisons against generation baselines are arguably unfair: VRDAG offers no explicit generation-size control, so it is evaluated 'on the graphs actually generated' at whatever scale it produces, while GAG-General generates exactly 2,000 edges; DG-Gen's ratio is hand-adjusted. Differences in MMD may largely reflect graph size rather than quality.

Overstated claims relative to evidence: statements such as 'groundbreaking results' and 'GDGB establishes robust benchmarks' are not matched by the modest, inconsistent results (e.g., several failed power-law validity checks under IDGG, MMDs above 0.3 for several datasets, and large variance across LLM backbones, with DeepSeek producing near-zero Hit@1 in some configurations). No statistical significance testing or variance over repeated runs is reported.

The central 'empirical insight' — that structural and textual features both matter for DyTAG generation — is unsurprising and only demonstrated through a single-model w/ vs. w/o-text MMD experiment (VRDAG/DG-Gen), which is a weak evidence base for a benchmark paper whose main contribution is empirical guidance.

Legal/ethical concerns around data provenance: several datasets are scraped in violation of restrictive terms (the IMDB license text quoted in Appendix A.2 explicitly prohibits reproduction and redistribution of scraped content; Weibo data is similarly scraped). Hosting redistributions on Kaggle may infringe these licenses, and the Broader Impact section does not address this specific risk.

Practicality of the framework is questionable: generating 10,000 edges takes ~1.6 hours and 100,000 edges takes 16-36 hours with an expensive LLM pipeline, yet no cost analysis or discussion of inference expenses is provided, which limits the benchmark's usability for the community it targets.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: there is currently no standardized benchmark for generative tasks on dynamic text-attributed graphs, and the proposed TDGG/IDGG task formulations (transductive vs. inductive generation) are sensible and well-motivated by real-world graph growth patterns.

The dataset contribution is substantial: eight curated DyTAG datasets spanning bipartite and non-bipartite graphs across multiple domains, with rich node- and edge-level text, documented licenses, statistics, and comparisons against prior datasets (Table 11). Public hosting of datasets, code, prompts, and leaderboards supports reproducibility.

The empirical validation that textual quality matters is convincing: Figure 2/6-7 show that on GDGB, adding text features consistently reduces Degree/Spectra MMD for VRDAG and DG-Gen, whereas on DTGB the effect is mixed — this cleanly demonstrates the textual-quality problem in prior datasets and motivates the benchmark.

The evaluation protocol is reasonably multifaceted, combining structural metrics (MMD, power-law validity), an LLM-as-Evaluator framework with five defined criteria, and an extended JL-Metric that jointly assesses structural, temporal, and textual fidelity.

The experimental coverage is broad: four LLM backbones, five DGNN baselines for discriminative tasks, two feature-supportive generation baselines (DG-Gen, VRDAG), ablations on node memory and reflection mechanisms, and scalability analyses in the appendix. Appendix material (pseudocode, prompts, implementation details, full result tables) is thorough.
weaknesses: The graph embedding metric results appear internally inconsistent or at least ambiguously reported: the metric rho is defined so that lower values indicate higher fidelity (Section B.2), yet in Tables 10 and 46 the authors bold 'Ours' (e.g., 0.661) over VRDAG's 0.011 as the best result, which would only be correct if higher is better. Either the metric direction or the interpretation needs clarification; as written, the headline claim that GAG-General 'significantly outperforms' VRDAG and DG-Gen on graph embedding quality is not clearly supported.

The discriminative-task comparison in TDGG is arguably unfair to the DGNN baselines: they are trained on only 1,000 edges while GAG-General sees the same seed graph via prompting with an LLM's pretrained knowledge. Concluding that 'DGNNs over-rely on large training input' from this setting overstates the finding; no DGNN results at matched data budgets or with larger training sets are provided to contextualize the comparison.

The LLM-as-Evaluator textual metric has a circularity/self-preference risk: GPT is both one of the generation backbones and the evaluator backbone, and all scores cluster tightly around 4-5 with no human evaluation to validate that the metric discriminates meaningful differences in text quality. Claims that memory/reflection 'significantly improves' textual quality rest on deltas of ~0.1-0.5 on an unvalidated 1-5 scale, without variance or significance testing.

Baseline comparisons for IDGG are apples-to-oranges in places: DG-Gen and VRDAG are trained only on a 1,000-edge seed graph, and VRDAG lacks generation-size control, so generated graph sizes (and hence MMD/embedding metrics) are not directly comparable across methods.

Generated-graph scale is small relative to the datasets' potential: experiments generate 10,000 (TDGG) and 2,000 (IDGG) edges from 1,000-edge seeds, and generation is slow (16-36 hours for 50k-100k edges). This limits the demonstrated scalability of the framework and the benchmark's immediate usefulness for million-edge datasets.

Dataset construction has quality-control concerns: IMDB's temporal span extends to 2031 (future films), which is problematic for a benchmark on modeling graph evolution; WikiLife's span is written as '202 to 2024' (typo); IMDB has only 122 timestamps, and several claimed licenses (e.g., Weibo/Dianping as CC-BY) are asserted for data scraped from commercial platforms, which the brief broader-impact section does not fully address.

Claims of 'groundbreaking results' (Section 6) are stronger than the evidence; the framework's structural fidelity in IDGG degrades notably (many datasets fail power-law validity), and the paper appropriately acknowledges the pipeline needs refinement, but the narrative tone is inconsistent with this.

strengths: Addresses a clear and genuine gap: existing DyTAG datasets have poor textual quality and there is no standardized generative DyTAG task formulation or evaluation protocol, making the benchmark timely and relevant.

The dataset collection effort is substantial: eight datasets spanning diverse domains, both bipartite and non-bipartite structures, with rich node/edge texts, documented licenses, and detailed statistics in the appendix.

The proposed TDGG/IDGG task split (transductive vs. inductive node generation) is well-motivated and better reflects real-world incremental graph growth than prior 'generate the final graph' formulations.

Evaluation is multifaceted (structural MMD/power-law, LLM-based textual scoring, extended JL-Metric), and the paper provides extensive experiments: four LLM backbones, ablations on memory/reflection, comparisons against DGNNs and graph-generation baselines, scalability analysis, downstream usability, data augmentation utility, semantic-drift analysis, and a human evaluation.
Reproducibility appears well-supported: datasets, code, prompts (G.1–G.3), implementation details, leaderboards, ethics statement, and disclosure of LLM usage are all provided.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in the framework: GAG-General is largely a domain-generalized extension of the existing GAG (Ji et al., 2025), with the architectural contributions (node memory, reflection) inherited or incremental; the main contribution is benchmark curation rather than methodological innovation.

Potential circularity in textual quality evaluation: the LLM-as-Evaluator scoring LLM-generated content may exhibit self-preference bias, and the evaluation criteria are adapted from role-playing agent research; the comparison to BERTScore is asserted rather than validated (e.g., no human study correlating the LLM evaluator with human judgment on generated texts).

Comparisons in the discriminative setting are arguably unfair/uninformative: DGNN baselines are trained on only 1,000 edges while GAG-General uses an LLM with world knowledge; concluding GAG-General 'outperforms DGNNs' from this low-data regime may overstate the framework's value, and gains on node retrieval are in fact minimal.

Limited scale of the generative evaluation: IDGG experiments target only 2,000 edges and generation times are high (up to tens of hours for 50K edges), leaving open questions about whether conclusions hold at the million-edge scale the datasets enable.

Several evaluation design choices are weak: power-law validity is a coarse binary criterion; some structural results are inconsistent (e.g., IMDB and WeiboDaily fail validity); no statistical significance or variance reporting for the graph metrics; and 'Ours' results in baseline comparisons are cherry-picked as the best across four LLM backbones.

Dataset quality issues remain: text enrichment relies on crawled Wikipedia paragraphs of varying relevance; WikiLife has very few timestamps (1,810) relative to its size, and there are typographical/consistency problems (e.g., temporal span '202 to 2024'; IMDB spanning to 2031 raises questions about using future-dated metadata).

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: standardized task formulations and evaluation protocols for generative DyTAG learning, which has been largely unexplored relative to discriminative dynamic graph tasks.

The benchmark is substantial in scale: eight datasets across diverse domains (e-commerce, social, citation, biography, web interaction), covering both bipartite and non-bipartite graphs, with rich node and edge textual attributes.
The two proposed tasks (transductive TDGG and inductive IDGG) are well-motivated, with IDGG's new-node generation plausibly modeling real-world open-ended graph growth.

Evaluation design is broad: structural (Degree/Spectra MMD, power-law), textual (multi-criterion LLM scoring), and a holistic graph-embedding metric, plus ablations on memory/reflection, scalability analysis, downstream usability tests, data-augmentation experiments, and a small human evaluation.

Extensive experimental coverage with multiple LLM backbones (DeepSeek, Llama, Qwen, GPT-4o-Mini) and comparisons to DGNNs and dynamic graph generation baselines; the appendix includes prompts, licenses, and reproducibility details.
The paper is generally well organized, with clear task definitions and pseudocode for the generation pipelines.
weaknesses: Circularity and bias in the primary evaluation: the textual quality metric relies on an LLM-as-Evaluator (GPT) judging text largely generated by LLM agents, including GPT itself; known self-preference effects are not addressed, and the consistently high scores (4.0-5.0) with narrow spreads suggest the metric may be insensitive. No validation of the LLM metric against large-scale human judgments is provided.

Baseline comparisons are constructed to favor the proposed method: DGNN baselines are trained on only 1,000 edges, then conclusions about GAG-General's superiority (particularly on edge classification) are drawn from this handicapped regime; no experiment shows DGNNs with realistic training data, so claims about DGNNs' 'limited generalization' are not well supported.

Scale and scope of experiments are limited: generation is restricted to 1,000-edge seeds producing 2,000-10,000-edge graphs, which is small relative to the million-edge datasets; many headline claims (e.g., 'groundbreaking performance' in Section 6) are stronger than the evidence.

Limited novelty of the framework: GAG-General is essentially a domain-generalization of GAG (Ji et al., 2025); its technical contribution beyond removing the bipartite constraint and abstracting the pipeline appears modest, so the paper's core novelty rests mainly on the dataset and task definitions.

Data quality and licensing concerns: several datasets are scraped (Wikipedia, IMDB, Weibo, Dianping), and the license claims for commercial/aggregated content (e.g., IMDB) are questionable; the IMDB dataset includes future events (up to 2031, 'Avatar 3'), which raises leakage and temporal-consistency issues; WikiLife's temporal span contains an apparent error ('202 to 2024').

The 'first generative DyTAG benchmark' claim is overstated: DTGB already includes a generative textual relation task, and GAG itself provides simulation-based DyTAG generation; positioning should be more precise.

Metric design weaknesses: the power-law validity criterion uses arbitrary thresholds (Dk < 0.15, alpha in [2,3]); the graph embedding metric produces noisy, inconsistent results across configurations (e.g., reflection sometimes degrades performance in Tables 4 and 7) without explanation; no statistical significance testing is reported for the many close comparisons.

The provided dataset/code URLs are blank in the abstract and reproducibility statement, hindering verification of reproducibility claims at review time; the small human study (5 annotators, 50 samples) and the 'Human-amenity Check' naming/typo suggest insufficient polish in the evaluation protocol.
The paper's claimed 'empirical insights' (structural and textual features are both crucial) are largely expected and demonstrate limited analytical depth beyond confirming the benchmark is usable.

strengths: Clear and meaningful contribution: GDGB is presented as the first generative DyTAG benchmark, addressing a genuine gap—prior resources (DTGB, TGB, DyGLib) support discriminative tasks but lack semantically rich node/edge texts and standardized generative task formulations.

The dataset curation work is substantial: eight datasets spanning e-commerce, social, web interaction, biographical, movie, and citation domains, with both bipartite and non-bipartite structures, documented sources, licenses, and preprocessing. The comparison against DTGB (Table 9, Figure 5, Table 10) provides concrete evidence that GDGB's textual attributes are richer (lower PPL, higher LLM ratings) and functionally useful (text features reduce MMD on GDGB but often degrade it on DTGB).

The two task formulations (TDGG and IDGG) are well-motivated: IDGG's inductive new-node generation models open-ended graph growth, which is more realistic than one-shot final-graph generation, and the tasks are formally specified with pseudocode (Algorithms 1–2).

Evaluation is comprehensive for a benchmark paper: structural metrics (MMD, power-law validity), LLM-based textual scoring, an extended JL-Metric embedding indicator, ablations over node memory/reflection and four LLM backbones, comparison with DG-Gen/VRDAG/TIGGER-I, downstream usability of generated graphs, data-augmentation utility (Table 54), semantic-drift analysis, and a small human evaluation.

Reproducibility efforts are above average: code, data, prompt templates (Sections G.1–G.3), implementation details, scalability/time-cost analysis, and ethics/reproducibility statements are all provided.
weaknesses: Evaluation circularity / self-preferential design: the benchmark's tasks, metrics, and primary evaluated framework all come from the same authors. The LLM-as-Evaluator textual metric borrows role-playing criteria (Personality Depth, Immersive Quality) that are not obviously suited to graph edge texts, is scored by GPT which is likely biased toward LLM-generated (especially GPT-generated) text, and is never validated against human judgment on a large scale (the human check covers only 50 samples on one task). The main conclusion—GAG-General generates the best DyTAGs—partly follows from metrics designed around that framework.

Baseline coverage for the generative tasks is thin. Only VRDAG, DG-Gen, and TIGGER-I are compared on IDGG, and none of them can produce text, so the comparison is structurally lopsided; for TDGG, comparisons with DGNNs under a 1,000-edge training budget arguably test DGNNs in an artificially data-starved regime rather than establishing generative superiority. No strong generative alternative (e.g., fine-tuned smaller LLMs, diffusion-based dynamic generators) is evaluated.

Some metric choices are arbitrary or weakly justified: the power-law validity criterion (Dk < 0.15 and α ∈ [2,3]) is a hard threshold that misclassifies several datasets; the graph embedding metric's cosine similarity lacks interpretation anchors (what score is 'good'?); and no statistical significance or variance analysis is reported for the LLM-as-Evaluator scores across runs.

Novelty of GAG-General is incremental: it is an extension of GAG (Ji et al., 2025) with generalization to non-bipartite graphs and abstraction of domain logic; the technical novelty is limited, and the 'groundbreaking performance' language in Section 6 overclaims given the acknowledged weaknesses in structural fidelity and semantic drift (Figure 12 shows drift after 5K edges).

Costs and practicality: generation is slow (16–36 hours for 50K–100K edges) and depends on large proprietary/open LLMs, raising questions about who can actually use the benchmark to develop new methods, and about dataset licensing/privacy (IMDB's terms, user-generated Weibo/Dianping content) which are described but the privacy risks of releasing raw user texts are not deeply addressed.

Presentation issues: the abstract's release URL is empty in the manuscript, several claims about GDGB 'outperforming DTGB' conflate dataset quality with framework performance, and the massive appendix (Tables 18–55) makes it difficult to identify which results are central versus exploratory.
